context: 1.4. Related Work Single-player multi-armed bandits were originally proposed by Thompson (1933) and asymptotically optimal strategies proposed by Lai and Robbins (1985), Cappé et al. (2013) amongst others. Building on the work of Lai and Robbins (1985), Anantharam et al. (1987) considered a generalization to the case where a single player can choose several arms, and proposed asymptotically optimal strategies. In fact, the problem considered by Anantharam et al. (1987) can be seen as a centralized version of the distributed problem we consider here. Motivated by wireless communication and networking, more recent works have considered multi-player multi-armed bandits, Liu and Zhao (2010), Rosenski et al. (2016), for instance as a natural model for a scenario where several players must access a wireless channel in a decentralized manner Besson and Kaufmann (2018). When collision sensing is available, several authors Boursier and Perchet (2019), Wang et al. (2020) have shown that one can obtain roughly the same performance as in the centralized case by cleverly exploiting collisions. A harder problem is the case without collision sensing. The state-of-the-art known algorithms for this problem are SIC-MMAB2 Boursier and Perchet (2019), EC-SIC Shi et al. (2020) and the algorithms of Lugosi and Mehrabian (2018). Our work improves on these algorithms, both in terms of performance, and in terms of practical applicability. Some generalizations and alternative settings were also considered. Bistritz and Leshem (2018) and Mehrabian et al. (2020) consider the more general heterogenous case where the mean of arms vary among players. Magesh and Veeravalli (2021) and Shi and Shen (2021) consider a variant of the probem where collisions can yield a non-zero reward. Bubeck et al. (2021) consider the additional assumption that players have access to shared randomness, and study the minimax regret. 1.5.
